prompt: Design a production-safe Linux performance engineering workflow for a multi-tenant Ubuntu service fleet. Cover the user outcome, experiment identity, controlled baseline, USE analysis across CPU/memory/storage/network, process and cgroup scope, counter semantics, profiling and tracing, security and overhead, hypothesis selection, sysctl/systemd/cgroup tuning, representative canaries, stop and rollback behavior, before/after statistics, sustained verification, drift and knowledge preservation.
directAnswer: Begin with a measurable user or batch outcome, exact workload and environment identity, stable traffic/request mix, repeated baseline distributions and explicit experiment ownership. Apply USE per resource: utilization, saturation and errors, at the boundary that owns demand and policy. Read counters as typed evidence with units, scope, collection mechanism, monotonic-versus-gauge behavior, reset/wrap and sampling limits. Move from broad symptoms to per-process/cgroup evidence and then to scoped on-CPU, off-CPU or event tracing only when a written hypothesis needs it. Measure profiler overhead and protect captured execution data. Change one versioned tunable or resource policy at a time in a representative canary, with exact semantics, expected mechanism, security/capacity impact, stop thresholds and tested rollback. Compare repeated distributions and confidence/variance under equivalent load, test user and neighbor outcomes, soak, detect drift, and record negative as well as positive results.
foundation: Performance engineering is causal experimentation under operational constraints. Utilization means busy time or resource occupancy; saturation means queued or delayed demand; errors mean failed operations or hardware/software faults. A counter has no meaning without boundary, unit, interval and collection semantics. Profiling says where samples landed, not automatically why users waited. Tuning is justified only when evidence identifies a mechanism and the change improves the named outcome without unacceptable reliability, security, capacity or cost regressions.
reasoningSteps: Name the operation, population and objective such as checkout p99 below 250 ms at 2,000 requests/s with errors below 0.1%, rather than 'make Linux faster'.
Define experiment ownership, maintenance window, blast radius, approver, stop authority, rollback target and evidence retention before collecting invasive data or changing state.
Bind workload identity: application and dependency versions, configuration, kernel/OS, host type, CPU topology, memory, devices, network, cgroup/systemd policy and hardening profile.
Control request mix, concurrency, data size, cache/warm-up state, dependency behavior and background work. Record unavoidable differences and do not call incomparable windows a baseline.
Collect repeated latency distributions, throughput, error/timeout results and resource evidence; averages alone hide tail behavior and multimodal workloads.
Inventory each resource and apply USE at the correct layer: host, NUMA node, device, interface, process, thread, cgroup and service.
For CPU, examine user/system/idle/steal accounting, per-CPU imbalance, runnable demand, context switches, throttling, PSI and machine or thermal errors.
For memory, distinguish capacity/working set/cache from pressure; inspect faults, reclaim, swap, PSI, cgroup events, OOM and hardware-error evidence.
For storage, identify exact filesystem/device path; examine throughput, utilization, queueing, latency distribution, writeback and device/filesystem errors.
For network, map the request path and inspect link utilization, queues/drops, retransmissions, connection backlog, latency and interface/driver errors.
Interpret every counter with unit, type, scope, interval, reset/wrap, kernel/tool version and collection limitations. Use deltas for monotonic counters.
Separate host resource shortage from workload policy. cgroup cpu.max, memory.high/max, io.max/weight and systemd properties can create local saturation while the host has headroom.
Write ranked hypotheses with predicted observations and disconfirming evidence. Choose the next command because it distinguishes hypotheses.

Use scoped profiling when aggregate evidence points to execution demand: perf stat for event counts, perf record/report for sampled on-CPU paths, off-CPU/wait analysis for blocked work and tracing for specific events/latency paths.
Validate PID start identity, cgroup, event availability, sample scope, symbol resolution, call graph mode, lost samples, multiplex scaling and measurement overhead.
Treat profile and trace artifacts as sensitive. Use least monitoring privilege, short duration, narrow process/cgroup/event filters, protected storage and controlled deletion.
Do not optimize a wide flame-graph frame blindly: frame width represents sampled frequency in the chosen profile, not inherent waste or a complete causal explanation.
For a proposed tunable, read exact kernel/vendor semantics and current/default value; state the mechanism, expected user/resource delta, compatibility and security implications.
Prefer application or architecture fixes when the bottleneck is algorithmic, lock/contention, excessive work or dependency behavior; kernel tuning cannot repair every code path.
Change one variable. Use a representative canary with sufficient traffic and the same dependencies, not an idle node or synthetic path that omits the bottleneck.
Declare user, resource, neighbor, error, security, thermal/power and cost stop thresholds before rollout. Automate halt where practical.
Capture the previous value and prove rollback in the same control plane. Avoid a recovery path that depends on the service or policy being changed.
Compare repeated before/after distributions under equivalent conditions; report sample count, variance or uncertainty, effect size and negative results.
Verify intended service behavior plus prohibited security behavior. A performance win does not justify silently expanding privilege, exposure or data collection.
Soak across burst, scheduled job, cache, failover and traffic phases. Watch for delayed writeback, reclaim, thermal throttling, starvation, cost and neighbor regressions.
Roll out in bounded waves, reconcile actual state, detect configuration drift and keep a time-bound exception if the fleet cannot converge immediately.
Store the experiment question, identities, commands, raw evidence, interpretation, change, result, rollback and review trigger so future engineers do not repeat folklore.
seniorAnswer: I run Linux performance work as a controlled evidence loop. First I pin a user outcome, request mix and exact workload/environment identity and collect repeated comparable distributions. Then I apply USE to CPU, memory, storage and network at host, process and cgroup boundaries, treating every counter as typed data with units, interval and limitations. That keeps me from reading host idle as proof that a quota-bound service has capacity. Profiling comes only after a hypothesis: scoped on-CPU samples for execution, off-CPU or event tracing for waits, with symbol/loss/overhead validation and least-privilege handling of sensitive artifacts. Any sysctl, systemd or cgroup change has exact versioned semantics, one variable, a representative canary, predeclared user/neighbor/security gates and proven rollback. I compare repeated before/after distributions, soak for delayed effects, expand in bounded waves and monitor drift. The output is an owned experiment record, including failed hypotheses—not a list of magic values.
weakAnswer: Install every monitoring tool, capture perf for the whole fleet, apply the throughput-performance profile, increase kernel queues and memory limits, then keep settings that improve average CPU.
whyWeak: It has no user objective, workload identity, controlled baseline or hypothesis; confuses CPU with user performance; over-collects sensitive data; changes multiple broad controls; ignores policy boundaries, tail latency, errors, neighbors, security, rollback and delayed regressions.

evidence.signal: Versioned experiment manifest and repeated user baseline
evidence.proves: Which outcome, workload, environment and distributions were observed
evidence.doesNotProve: The root cause or future behavior

evidence.signal: USE evidence by resource and boundary
evidence.proves: Observed utilization, delayed demand and errors within stated scopes
How evidence was interpreted and compared

evidence.signal: Scoped profile or trace with symbols/loss/overhead
evidence.proves: Sampled execution or event behavior for one interval and scope
evidence.doesNotProve: Complete execution, wall time or user causality

evidence.signal: One-variable canary with stop and rollback record
evidence.proves: Observed response and reversibility in the canary
Measured effect and selected regressions under comparable conditions
Observed persistence and state convergence in covered periods/assets

followUps.prompt: How do utilization and saturation differ?
followUps.answer: Utilization describes time busy or resource occupancy; saturation describes work queued or delayed beyond immediate service. A CPU can be highly utilized without harmful queueing, and a quota-bound cgroup can be saturated while the host is underutilized.

followUps.prompt: When should you use an on-CPU versus off-CPU profile?
followUps.answer: Use on-CPU samples when execution consumes CPU and you need hot stacks. Use off-CPU or event/wait tracing when wall time is dominated by sleep, lock, I/O, scheduling or dependency waits. The user symptom and process states choose the view.

followUps.prompt: Why change one tunable at a time?
followUps.answer: It preserves attribution and makes rollback precise. Multiple simultaneous changes can cancel or amplify each other, hide security or reliability regressions and prevent a defensible causal conclusion.

followUps.prompt: Can a tuned profile be the final answer?
followUps.answer: No. A profile encodes workload assumptions and multiple settings. Inspect its exact version and contents, test it as a change set against the named workload and preserve a revert path. Ubuntu explicitly frames profiles as starting points.

followUps.prompt: What does a flame graph prove?
followUps.answer: Within the selected scope, period, event, stack mode and successful samples, width represents sample frequency in stack paths. It does not by itself prove waste, waiting time, causality, latency contribution or optimization safety.

rubric.observableEvidence: Defines user objective, identity, controlled load, distributions and ownership
Covers accounting, run queues, throttling, pressure, topology and errors
Separates capacity, working set, reclaim, pressure, limits and errors
Maps exact paths and evaluates utilization, queues, latency, drops/retransmits and errors
Binds host/process/cgroup and handles units, deltas, reset and limitations
Chooses on/off-CPU or events, validates symbols/loss/overhead and interprets cautiously
Uses least privilege, protects artifacts and refuses unjustified control weakening
Verifies semantics, changes one variable and uses representative canary/gates
Proves reversal and compares repeated user/resource/neighbor/security evidence
Soaks, rolls out in waves, detects drift and preserves reproducible records
